EE practice: plan the search with Tull (at least three kinds of source).
EE practice: use the Date Lens on all three pen exhibits.

locks.title: The Inventor's Share
locks.subject: business
locks.intro: A brass lock with three rings. Each ring holds part of a research question. The lock opens only for a question that is focused enough to research and open enough to argue. This is practice on a set topic. It is not your own Extended Essay question.

options.why: 'Why did' assumes that the answer is yes. An argument needs room for 'not much' as an answer.
A yes-or-no question gives you one word to argue about. Ask how far, or to what extent.
'Technology' is everything at once. Choose one thing that you can find sources about.

options.text: who was credited for the ballpoint pen, from Loud's patent (1888) to the Bíró pen (1945 to 1948)?
who was paid for the ballpoint pen in the 1940s?
who was credited for every invention in history?
options.why: Every invention in history is too much for one essay. Choose one case with dates.
That is a topic, not a question about one case. Choose a case that sources can answer.

locks.openLine: Click. The rings lock together. The question is focused, has a case with dates, and leaves room to argue both ways.

criteria.text: decided who was credited for the ballpoint pen
were one factor in who was credited for the ballpoint pen
mattered less than who made a pen that worked and sold

limits.text: Counterclaim: a patent shows that a claim was granted, not that a pen worked or sold.
Counterclaim: the dates in these records answer different questions.

supports.subject: patents
supports.heard: Tull reads it twice. 'One factor, with a counterclaim that you answer. That is an argument, not a list.'

supports.subject: patents
supports.heard: Tull nods. 'You put the patent in its place, and you say what you put in its place. Good.'

supports.subject: records
supports.heard: Tull smiles. 'Records shape memory. And you can show it with the records themselves.'

supports.subject: records
supports.heard: Tull taps the desk. 'A careful claim. The records only show part of the story, and you say so.'

supports.subject: patents
supports.heard: Tull reads it. It holds, for now.
supports.weak: Tull frowns. 'Decided? Loud had the patent, and the pens people remember are Bíró's. Your own cards argue against you.'

supports.subject: records
supports.heard: Tull reads it. It holds, for now.
supports.weak: Tull frowns. 'A museum record decided it? The record came after the pen. What decided the record?'

weak.noSupport: Tull reads it aloud. 'Which of your cards says this? A claim with no support is a guess in a nice font.'
weak.tooStrong: Tull reads it in a flat voice, the way visitors repeat the old label. 'It sounds strong. Your evidence says something smaller.'

legends.intro: Build the main claim of a practice argument. A bigger claim needs more support. A counterclaim that you answer makes a claim more careful. More than one claim can hold.
legends.subject: What made the difference
legends.button: Put the claim on the board

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Not now, Guardian. Repair the old label first. Then come and see me: I have a lock that only opens for good questions.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: You repaired the label. Good. Now: an essay is a long label with an argument. Want to practise? This lock is the first step. It only opens for a question that you could really research.

options.text: Is this my real Extended Essay?

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: No. Your real essay is your own work, with a supervisor at school. This is practice on a topic I chose: the ballpoint pen. Nothing you do here goes into your real essay, and I will never suggest a topic for it.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: The lock is still waiting. Three rings: a question word, what made the difference, and one case with dates.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: The lock is open. Now plan the search. Where would you look first? Choose as many as you like. I'll tell you what this archive holds.

options.text: A history from a patent office.
As many web pages as I can find.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: We hold the record of US patent 392,046, granted to John J. Loud in 1888. Keywords that help: the patent number, the name, the grant date.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: We hold the Science Museum Group record for a Biro pen, 1945 to 1948. A museum record tells you about one object, not the whole story.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: We hold the German patent office's history of the ballpoint pen. It separates Loud's patent from the Bíró brothers' later work.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: This archive has no company or licence records. A real search would need them to say who was paid. Write down that this is a gap. Knowing what you lack is part of the plan.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Many pages copy one page. Ten copies of one claim are still one source. Ask where each page got its claim.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: A plan with kinds of source, and a gap that you can name. Now weigh what we hold. Use your Date Lens on all three pen exhibits: each date answers a different question.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Use the Date Lens on all three pen exhibits in the hall. For each one, ask: what does this source show, and what can it not show?

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: You have weighed the sources. Now build the argument on my claim board: a claim, a counterclaim that you answer, and support from your cards. More than one claim can hold.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Now cite. Your argument says that Loud's patent was granted in 1888. Which record do you cite for that?

options.text: US Patent 392,046, J. J. Loud, granted 30 October 1888.
The Science Museum Group record of a Biro pen, 1945 to 1948.
A web page that copies the patent drawing.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: That record is about a pen made between 1945 and 1948. It says nothing about 1888. A citation must point to the record that supports this exact claim.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Go to the original record when you can. A copy can drop or change details, and your reader needs to check the original.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Good. Second claim: Bíró developed a practical pen with his brother György and others. Which record?

options.text: The German patent office's history of the ballpoint pen.
Everyone knows it. It needs no citation.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Loud's patent is from 1888. It cannot tell you anything about the Bíró brothers in the 1930s and 1940s.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: 'Everyone knows' is how the old label started. If a reader could ask 'says who?', cite it.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Two claims, two records, each one checkable. Use your school's citation style for real work. The habit is the same: say where each claim comes from.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: One more thing. Someone left this practice draft in the reading room. It has three problems. Can you find them?

options.text: The second paragraph is word for word from the museum label, with no quotation marks.
'Bíró, Memoirs of the First Pen (1931)' is not in any catalogue. Did a machine invent it?

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Yes. Copied words need quotation marks and a citation, or they need to be your own words. Otherwise it is someone else's work under your name.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Yes. I searched every catalogue: no such book. A text generator made up a title that sounds right. Check that every source exists before you cite it.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Yes. A date is a claim. The reader needs to know which record gives it.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Read it again, slowly. Ask of each sentence: whose words, and which source?

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: All three. You would be a good examiner of your own work, and that is the point.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Last step, and the one people skip. What changed in your thinking on this trail? There is no wrong answer. I'll put it in your portfolio, and you can add your own words there.

options.text: My question got smaller, and better.
I found out what the archive does not hold.
A counterclaim made my argument stronger, not weaker.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: Noted. 'Not sure yet' is an honest reflection too. Open your portfolio (P) to add your own words. Only you decide whether your teacher sees it.

dialogue.speaker: archivist-tull
dialogue.text: The lock remembers your question. Practice is for building habits. Your real essay will be your own, with your supervisor.

options.text: Can I try the lock again?

hints.text: The lock wants a question you could research and argue.
Avoid questions that assume the answer, or that ask yes or no.
Pick one thing that made a difference, and one case with dates.
Try: 'To what extent did' + 'patents decide' + 'who was credited for the ballpoint pen…'.
Think about kinds of source, not single pages.
Which records would show a patent, an object, or a payment?
Choose at least three kinds of source with Tull, then say 'That is my plan'.
Talk to Tull. Choose 'Patent records', 'Museum object records' and 'A history from a patent office', then 'That is my plan'.
Each date answers a different question.
The Date Lens is in your bag. Use it at an exhibit.
Use the Lens on the patent drawing, the workshop model and the Biro pen record.
Walk to each of the three pedestals in the main hall, inspect it, and press 'Use the Date Lens'.
A strong essay claim is not the loudest claim.
A counterclaim that you answer makes a claim more careful.
Choose 'were one factor' or 'mattered less', add a counterclaim, and use your cards.
Talk to Tull, open the claim board: 'Patents' + 'were one factor…' + the first counterclaim.
Every claim needs the record that supports it.
Match the date or the name to the record that really says it.
1888 is in the patent record. The Bíró brothers are in the patent office history.
Talk to Tull. Choose 'US Patent 392,046…', then 'The German patent office's history…'.
Read the draft as if you were the examiner.
Look for borrowed words, a source that does not exist, and a claim without a source.
There are three problems: a copied paragraph, an invented book, a date without a citation.
Talk to Tull and choose each of the three problems, then 'That is all three'.
Look back at where you started.
Any honest answer counts, including 'not sure yet'.
Talk to Tull and choose what changed in your thinking.
Talk to Tull and choose any of the four answers.

journal.text: EE practice: the Title Lock opened. A good research question is focused, has one case with dates, and leaves room to argue.
EE practice trail finished: question, search plan, weighing, argument with counterclaim, citations, integrity check, reflection. Practice only. My real essay is my own work.
